strengths: Novel and interpretable framing of multimodal RLVR through token-level 'visual dependency,' operationalized via KL divergence between output distributions conditioned on original vs. masked images.
Two well-motivated empirical insights (sparsity of visually-dependent tokens; heterogeneity of trajectory-level visual grounding) that directly justify the proposed method rather than being post-hoc.
VPPO is simple and modular—can be plugged into GRPO/DAPO—with a clear dual mechanism (trajectory-level advantage shaping + token-level gradient filtering).

Extensive empirical validation across eight diverse benchmarks (math, geometry, logic, multi-discipline) and two model scales (7B, 32B), with consistent and often substantial gains over strong open-source RL-tuned baselines.

Thorough ablation studies covering masking strategy, dependency metric choice (KL vs JSD vs Top-1 drop), entropy penalty, rollout group size, filtering ratio k, and shaping range, which support the design choices.

Comparison against entropy-based pivotal token selection (a natural competing baseline from text-only LLM literature) strengthens the case that visual dependency is a more suitable signal for multimodal settings.
Qualitative case studies are illustrative and show plausible correction of baseline reasoning errors.
weaknesses: The theoretical variance-reduction analysis (Theorem 3.1) relies on several strong, somewhat unrealistic assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, independence of advantage/shaping factor from gradients, second-moment dominance) and reads more as a heuristic justification than a rigorous guarantee; its practical relevance is unclear.

Computing token visual dependency requires an additional forward pass with masked images for every token in every rollout trajectory, which is a non-trivial overhead; the reported ~10% wall-clock increase is not fully substantiated with memory/compute analysis, and details of how masked-image distributions are efficiently obtained during rollout are sparse.

Baseline comparisons mix reproduced numbers (with author-provided prompts) and numbers taken directly from other papers (e.g., PAPO-D), raising potential concerns about strict comparability/fairness across methods under a single evaluation pipeline.

The ablation in Table 2 shows that combining TAS+TGF is not uniformly better than TGF alone (e.g., worse on DynaMath, Geo3k, MathVision, LogicVista), which somewhat undercuts the claimed 'synergistic value' of the hierarchical design.

No variance/seed information is reported for training runs, despite RL training being known to be sensitive to seed and initialization; only avg@8 at inference is reported, which addresses evaluation stochasticity but not training variance.
Key hyperparameters (k=0.4, β range) appear tuned on the same benchmark suite used for final evaluation, raising a mild risk of overfitting to the specific benchmark distribution.

The visual dependency metric could be confounded by token position or generic distributional sensitivity to any perturbation (not necessarily reasoning-relevant), and this potential confound is not explicitly ruled out.

The second core insight (that trajectories vary in visual groundedness) is somewhat expected/intuitive, and the main technical novelty resides primarily in the specific token-level scoring and its integration into the RL objective.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated perspective for multimodal RLVR: quantifying token-level 'visual dependency' via KL divergence between output distributions conditioned on original vs. perturbed (masked) visual input, and using this signal to shape both trajectory-level advantages (TAS) and token-level gradient masks (TGF).

Extensive empirical validation across 8 diverse benchmarks (math, geometry, logic, multi-discipline) and two model scales (7B and 32B), consistently outperforming strong open-source RL-tuned baselines (DAPO, GRPO, MM-Eureka, VL-Rethinker, PAPO, NoisyRollout, etc.).

Very thorough ablation studies: TAS vs. TGF individually and combined; sensitivity to filtering ratio k and shaping range; comparison of dependency-calculation metrics (KL vs JSD vs Top-1 prob drop); comparison of masking/perturbation strategies (patch blackening vs noise vs blur vs full masking); binary vs soft masks; advantage vs reward shaping; generalization to GRPO as base algorithm; rollout group size; entropy-penalty stabilization analysis; and out-of-domain VQA generalization.

Provides a theoretical variance-reduction argument (Theorem 3.1) connecting the sparsity ratio and shaping factor to reduced gradient variance, complementing the empirical training-stability observations.

Good transparency/reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, training procedure pseudocode, computational overhead analysis (only ~10% extra cost) including an equal-time-budget comparison showing gains are not simply due to extra compute, and qualitative case studies contrasting VPPO with baseline failure modes.

The insights (sparse token-level visual dependency; heterogeneous trajectory-level visual grounding) are intuitively appealing and well-illustrated with qualitative examples, providing interpretability alongside performance gains.
weaknesses: The theoretical variance-reduction analysis (Theorem 3.1) relies on several strong, unrealistic independence assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, advantage independent of gradients, dependency independent of advantage), so the 'proof' is more of a rough intuition-building exercise than a rigorous guarantee.

The core dependency metric is based on KL divergence between original and masked-image output distributions; this conflates true visual grounding with generic sensitivity to any large, potentially out-of-distribution perturbation to the input (masked images may look unnatural to the model), which is not fully disentangled despite the masking-strategy ablation.

Some benchmark-level results are mixed rather than uniformly improved (e.g., MMK12 and DynaMath at 32B scale are essentially on par with or slightly below DAPO), which is somewhat understated in the narrative that emphasizes uniform superiority.

Baseline numbers for many competitors are self-reported reproductions (marked with †) rather than official published numbers, raising some concern about comparison fairness, although this is a common and largely unavoidable practice.

Experiments are limited to a single training dataset (ViRL39K) and to reasoning-centric benchmarks; applicability to other data distributions or more subjective/creative multimodal tasks (as the authors themselves note) is untested.

Scaling is only validated up to 32B; behavior at larger scales (e.g., 70B+) remains unverified, and the hyperparameters (k, β range, masking probability) appear tuned specifically to this setup, requiring re-tuning for new settings.
